title: Shopify vs Adobe Stock: The Ecommerce Buy Decision in APAC
summary: Shopify vs Adobe stock ecommerce buy decisions for APAC enterprise retailers: platform differentiation, vendor momentum, real costs and five-year risk assessment.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Shopify grew GMV 32% in Q3 2025 as a pure-play commerce vendor; Adobe is larger but discloses Commerce inside a broader segment. For APAC platform buyers, Shopify Plus suits predictable, fast-moving DTC; Adobe Commerce suits multi-entity, deep-B2B operations with in-house engineering.


---


Shopify reported $92.1 billion in GMV in Q3 2025, up 32% year over year, while Adobe's Digital Experience subscription revenue — the segment that contains Adobe Commerce — grew roughly 10% over its FY2025, according to each company's investor relations disclosures. That gap is the single most useful data point most platform buyers never look at. If you typed "Shopify vs Adobe stock ecommerce buy" into a search bar, you probably wanted one of two things: an equity call, or a platform decision. For a retail operator in Hong Kong, Singapore, Sydney or Taipei signing a five-year commerce commitment, those two questions are closer than they look.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus Cross-Border Repeat Customer Growth: The 149% Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-cross-border-repeat-customer-growth-149-playbook)


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Marketing Cloud CDP Strategy: An APAC Retail Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-marketing-cloud-cdp-strategy-apac-retail)


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus B2B Replatforming Guide for APAC Distributors](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-b2b-replatforming-guide-apac)


I spend my days on the second question — which platform a listed retailer, a multi-brand catering group, or a manufacturer with a dealer network should run on for the next half-decade. But I read the first question's data because it tells me where R&D dollars are going, which partner networks are growing, and which roadmap is likely to still matter in 2030. Vendor momentum is a procurement input, not just a trading signal.


*Related reading:*[L'Oréal CDP Rollout Consumer Spend Uplift: The Real Numbers](https://branch8.com/posts/loreal-cdp-rollout-consumer-spend-uplift-apac-benchmarks)


## The stock chart is a vendor-risk document


When you buy a commerce platform, you are underwriting a bet that the vendor keeps investing in it. Replatforming a mid-sized APAC retailer is rarely a three-month job: catalogue migration, payment and logistics reintegration, ERP and POS plumbing, and staff retraining typically run two to four quarters before anything goes live. Amortise that over five years and the vendor's financial trajectory becomes material.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce AWS Integration for Global Growth: The APAC Play](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-aws-integration-global-growth-apac-data-warehouse)


Two things matter more than share price:


- **Segment disclosure.** Shopify is a pure-play commerce company — every dollar of its reported revenue depends on merchants succeeding. Adobe discloses Commerce inside the broader Digital Experience segment alongside Experience Manager, Analytics, Journey Optimizer and Marketo. You cannot isolate Commerce's growth from Adobe's filings. That opacity is not evidence of neglect, but it does mean you are reading tea leaves rather than numbers.
- **Where the engineering goes.** Adobe used its 2025 Summit to launch Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service (ACCS), a genuinely SaaS-delivered version of Commerce paired with Edge Delivery Services — a clear signal that Adobe sees its future in managed, composable delivery rather than self-hosted Magento installs. Shopify, meanwhile, spent 2024–2025 shipping Functions, Checkout Extensibility, Hydrogen/Oxygen, and the Catalyst/Commerce Components work aimed squarely at enterprise accounts.


Both vendors are moving in the same direction: away from monolithic self-hosting, towards managed services with extension points. They are just starting from opposite ends.


## What the momentum numbers actually say


Shopify's Q3 2025 results showed revenue of roughly $2.84 billion, up 32%, with gross merchandise volume growth tracking at a similar rate and payments penetration continuing to climb (Shopify Investor Relations). Adobe closed FY2025 at approximately $23.5 billion in total revenue with high-single to low-double-digit growth, driven heavily by Creative Cloud and Document Cloud (Adobe Investor Relations). Adobe is a much larger, more profitable, more diversified business. Shopify is a faster-growing, commerce-only business.


For the equity question, that is a genuine toss-up — Yahoo Finance has published credible arguments on both sides within the same quarter, one favouring Adobe's earnings momentum and cloud-native upgrades, another favouring Shopify's GMV growth and agentic commerce positioning. I have no edge there and will not pretend to.


For the platform question, the asymmetry matters differently. Adobe's size means Commerce competes internally for investment against Firefly, Creative Cloud and the broader AI roadmap. Shopify has no such internal competition. If you are a retailer whose entire business sits on the platform, concentrated vendor focus is worth something — though it also means your vendor has no diversified revenue cushion if commerce growth stalls.


On third-party adoption, BuiltWith's technology trend data has shown Shopify's share of the top million sites climbing steadily while Magento/Adobe Commerce installs decline — a pattern driven largely by Magento Open Source sites consolidating or migrating, not by Adobe's enterprise accounts leaving. Read it as a signal about the talent pool and agency supply, not about enterprise capability.

## Where Adobe Commerce still wins the architecture argument


I do not think Shopify wins every enterprise evaluation, and the APAC deals where Adobe Commerce is the right answer share recognisable traits.


**Native multi-entity, multi-store complexity.** Adobe Commerce's store/store-view/website hierarchy was built for this. One installation can serve Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore with separate tax rules, catalogues, price books and currencies while sharing a single admin and inventory source. Shopify Plus addresses this with expansion stores — the commonly cited allowance is up to around ten additional stores — but each is a separate instance. Cross-instance inventory, customer identity and reporting become integration work, a point Reddit threads on Shopify Plus vs Adobe Commerce have correctly hammered for years.


**Deep B2B.** Adobe ships company accounts, requisition lists, negotiable quotes, shared catalogues and tiered pricing natively. Shopify's B2B functionality has improved substantially since 2023 but a dealer network with multi-tier approval chains and account-specific price books usually still needs apps or custom work.


**Code-level control.** You can do things in Adobe Commerce you simply cannot do in Shopify — rewrite checkout logic, alter the order state machine, run custom indexers. A quick smell test: if your team is comfortable with


```text
1  bin/magento setup:upgrade    2  bin/magento indexer:reindex catalog_product_price    3  bin/magento cache:clean config full_page
```


and you have a reason to own that layer, Adobe is a real option. If that command block makes your CTO wince about who maintains it in year three, it isn't.


Shopify's answer to extensibility is narrower but safer. Business logic runs as sandboxed Functions at specific extension points rather than as core overrides:


```text
1  mutation {    2    cartLinesAdd(cartId: "gid://shopify/Cart/abc123", lines: [{merchandiseId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/456", quantity: 2}]) {    3      cart { id cost { totalAmount { amount currencyCode } } }    4    }    5  }
```


You get less control and far less upgrade risk. That is the whole trade, stated honestly.


## Is Shopify still worth it in 2026?


For most APAC retailers under roughly US$100 million in online revenue, yes — with two caveats that have grown sharper.


The first is cost drift. Shopify Plus list pricing starts in the region of $2,300–$2,500 per month on an annual term per Shopify's published plans, but the headline is rarely the bill. Add Shopify Payments processing (or a surcharge if you use an external gateway), app subscriptions that compound as you add subscriptions, loyalty, ERP connectors and reviews, plus agency retainers. I have seen app stacks on mid-market APAC stores exceed the platform licence itself. Shopify's own marketing claims its TCO is about 29% better than Adobe Commerce's on average — treat that as a vendor-funded figure and model your own.


The second is payment and logistics localisation. Shopify Payments availability varies by market across APAC, and in several territories you will run a local gateway alongside it. Octopus, FPS, PayMe, PromptPay, GrabPay, LINE Pay, TrueMoney, COD for Southeast Asia — the long tail of local payment methods is where generic platform comparisons stop being useful. Verify method-by-method for every market you sell into before you sign. Adobe Commerce has no inherent advantage here either; it just gives you more rope to build your own integration.

## The real cost picture for an APAC buyer


Strip out the marketing and a five-year comparison looks roughly like this in shape, if not in numbers you should trust from me:


- **Shopify Plus:** predictable licence, platform-included hosting and PCI scope, variable payments cost, app subscriptions that scale with feature count, lower build cost, higher per-feature cost at the margin. Upgrades happen to you, not by you.
- **Adobe Commerce (Cloud or ACCS):** licence commonly tiered by GMV — public reseller guidance has put entry tiers in the low tens of thousands of USD annually, rising steeply — plus infrastructure, plus a substantially larger build and maintenance line. More capability included, more responsibility retained.


The variable nobody models properly is **engineering supply** . In Hong Kong, Singapore and Taipei, experienced Magento developers are scarcer and more expensive than they were five years ago; Shopify-fluent developers are abundant but often shallow on enterprise integration. Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines remain the practical answer for sustained Adobe Commerce maintenance capacity, which is exactly why global brands increasingly run APAC-based delivery teams for platforms they operate in the US and EU. If your platform choice depends on hiring eight Magento engineers in Central, you have chosen the wrong platform for your location.


In one engagement with a Greater China jewellery retailer carrying a large SKU catalogue across multiple markets, the deciding factor was not feature parity at all — it was which platform their existing in-house team could still operate after the implementation partner walked away. That question answers more evaluations than any scorecard.


## What the top three ecommerce platforms look like from Asia


Ask this question in the US and you get Shopify, Adobe Commerce and BigCommerce or Salesforce. Ask it in APAC and the answer shifts. Shopify leads for brand-led DTC across Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Hong Kong. Adobe Commerce holds enterprise and B2B accounts with heavy customisation. The third slot is regional: SHOPLINE has real share across Greater China and Southeast Asia with native support for local payments, logistics and social commerce flows that global platforms treat as edge cases, while marketplace-first strategies on Shopee, Lazada and Tmall still dominate volume in much of Southeast Asia.


Gartner Peer Insights currently shows both vendors rated closely — Shopify around 4.5 stars and Adobe around 4.4 across several hundred reviews each — which should tell you that satisfaction is not the differentiator. Fit is.


For a US or UK brand entering Asia, the sequencing matters more than the platform: Shopify Plus for the brand storefront, a regional marketplace integration layer, and local payment rails bolted on. For an APAC group expanding outward, the question inverts — you are usually consolidating fragmented market-by-market stacks, and that is where Adobe's single-instance multi-store model earns a serious look.

## How to assess vendor risk before a five-year commitment


Four checks I run before signing anything:


1. **Read the roadmap commitments, not the keynote.** Adobe Experience League publishes release notes and lifecycle policies for Commerce versions; Shopify publishes developer changelogs and API versioning policies with explicit deprecation windows. Both are public. Check whether the capability you are buying is GA, beta, or a Summit slide.
2. **Check the partner network depth in your actual market.** Not the global count. How many certified partners can staff a project in Taipei or Jakarta next quarter?
3. **Model the exit.** What does data portability look like? Shopify's APIs and bulk export are straightforward for catalogue and orders; custom app data and checkout logic are not portable. Adobe Commerce's database is yours, which sounds better until you price migrating 400 custom modules.
4. **Stress-test the pricing clause.** GMV-tiered licensing means a good year raises your platform bill. Know the tier boundaries before you forecast.


Anyone framing a "Shopify vs Adobe stock ecommerce buy" decision purely on share-price momentum is solving the wrong problem. The equity question and the procurement question use some of the same evidence and reach different conclusions, and the procurement one is the only one your board will hold you accountable for.


## The honest limits of this advice


The direction of travel is clear enough: both vendors are converging on managed, API-first, AI-assisted commerce, and the differentiator over the next three years will be agentic checkout, catalogue intelligence and how cleanly each platform handles cross-border tax, payments and compliance in fragmented Asian markets. Shopify currently ships faster. Adobe currently bends further. Neither position is permanent.


This framing is not for everyone. If you are a pure-play marketplace seller in Southeast Asia, neither platform is your priority — your channel integrations are. If your online revenue is under roughly US$5 million, Adobe Commerce is almost certainly over-engineered for you regardless of what a feature matrix says. If you are an investor rather than an operator, nothing here is a stock recommendation; I have no position and no edge on either equity. And if you already run a stable, heavily customised Adobe Commerce install that your team maintains competently, the strongest argument for migrating is usually someone else's sales deck, not your P&L.
